CausalChain: Chronic liver inflammation and fibrosis -> Hepatocyte transformation and genomic instability -> Altered exosome biogenesis -> Enhanced secretion of specific microRNAs targeting HGF/MET and angiogenic pathways -> Promotion of tumor vascular invasion and immune evasion -> Changes in serum biomarker profiles (e.g., AFP variants, DCP) -> Differential therapeutic response to immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatments
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that chronic liver inflammation drives hepatocyte transformation and genomic instability, which in turn leads to altered exosome biogenesis. This alteration results in the enhanced secretion of a specific subset of microRNAs that modulate the HGF/MET and angiogenic pathways. The dysregulated miRNA profiles promote tumor vascular invasion and immune evasion, and correlate with distinct serum biomarker profiles (e.g., AFP variants and DCP). By employing advanced liquid biopsy platforms—including high-throughput exosome isolation, digital droplet PCR, next-generation sequencing, and integrative machine learning analysis—these exosomal miRNA signatures can be robustly quantified. Such enhanced profiling will enable early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and predict individual responses to immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatments, paving the way for personalized therapeutic interventions.
Abstract: This study hypothesizes that chronic liver inflammation initiates a cascade culminating in hepatocyte transformation, altered exosome biogenesis, and the enhanced secretion of microRNAs (miRNAs) that specifically modulate the HGF/MET and angiogenic pathways. These miRNA signatures, detectable in circulating exosomes, are proposed not only to underlie tumor vascular invasion and immune evasion but also to generate distinct serum biomarker profiles (including AFP variants and DCP). Leveraging state-of-the-art liquid biopsy techniques, digital droplet PCR, and next-generation sequencing integrated with machine learning, we aim to precisely quantify these exosome-derived miRNAs. This refined approach is expected to facilitate early diagnosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and enable the prediction of patient-specific responses to immunotherapy and anti-angiogenic treatments, thereby informing personalized therapeutic strategies.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis addressed the role of exosome-derived miRNAs, particularly those influencing the HGF/MET and angiogenesis pathways, as early diagnostic biomarkers and predictors of treatment response in HCC. The refined hypothesis maintains this core idea while explicitly outlining the causal chain: beginning with chronic liver inflammation, leading to hepatocyte transformation, altered exosome biogenesis, and the secretion of pathway-specific miRNAs. The new version further integrates modern technological capabilities—such as advanced liquid biopsy techniques, digital droplet PCR, next-generation sequencing, and machine learning—to enhance the practical implementability and robustness of biomarker quantification. This integration reinforces the mechanistic rationale provided by each step in the original causal chain while addressing technical challenges and emphasizing clinical applicability.
